column1: # Leave the id off a new row — omit the column entirely, do not leave it empty:
# a leading tab shifts every field one place left.
# Why this file is arranged by trigger rather than by topic. The subjunctive is
# not a meaning a learner can aim at; `sea` says nothing on its own about time,
# doubt or politeness. It is there because a word in front of it put it there.
# So the unit of learning is the pair — `quiero que` + form, `para que` + form —
# and grouping by pair is what lets a learner meet one trigger eight times in
# eight different sentences instead of eight triggers once each.
# The order is roughly the order these are worth teaching in: wanting something
# of another person first, because it is the one an English speaker already
# expresses with an infinitive and therefore gets wrong; then hoping, advising,
# doubting, reacting, purpose, future time; and the negative command last,
# because it is the one that looks like a tense the learner already has.

column2: Quiero que me ayudes con este archivo.
column3: I want you to help me with this file.
column6: English uses an infinitive here — «I want you to help». Spanish cannot: a second person needs a second clause.

column2: Ojalá no llueva mañana.
column3: I hope it does not rain tomorrow.
column6: «Ojalá» comes from the Arabic «law šāʾ Allāh», if God wills. It needs no verb of its own, and never takes the indicative.

column2: No creo que el riesgo sea tan grave.
column3: I do not think the risk is that serious.
column6: «Creo que es» takes the indicative; the doubt lives in the «no». Negating the belief is what moves the second verb.

column3: I am explaining it so that you understand the risk.
column6: «Para que» always takes the subjunctive: a purpose is by definition something that has not happened yet.

column2: Reciclamos para que el planeta esté mejor.
column3: We recycle so that the planet is in better shape.

column3: I am writing it down so that it is clear.

column3: I use an app so that I do not forget anything.

column2: Cuando llegues, llámame.
column3: When you arrive, call me.
column6: «Cuando llego» is a habit; «cuando llegue» is a single arrival still ahead. English uses one form for both.

column2: Te lo digo cuando tenga la respuesta.
column3: I will tell you when I have the answer.

column2: Hablamos cuando termines el proyecto.

column2: Cuando cobre, pago la factura.
column3: When I get paid, I will pay the bill.

column2: Mientras no haya una solución, no cambia nada.
column3: As long as there is no solution, we carry on as we are.

column2: Aunque sea complicado, vale la pena.
column3: Even if it is complicated, it is worth it.
column6: «Aunque» takes the indicative for a fact and the subjunctive for a concession: «aunque es tarde» admits it is; «aunque sea tarde» does not.

column2: Aunque no estés de acuerdo, es la decisión de todos.
column3: Even if you do not agree, it is the decision of all of us.

column2: Aunque el puesto sea temporal, da experiencia.
column3: Even if the post is temporary, it gives you experience.

column3: Even if the app is free, it has adverts.

column2: Aunque sea difícil, quiero intentarlo.
column3: Even if it is hard, I want to try.

column2: No te preocupes por la factura.
column3: Do not worry about the bill.
column6: The affirmative is «preocúpate», the negative «no te preocupes». Two different forms, and only the negative is the subjunctive.
